opus-5.5.text:
Part of it is just that we want robust answers. If you only ask one way, you don't know how much of the answer is about the question format rather than what people actually believe. And it turns out the framing matters a lot.

When we give people fixed years, like "what's the probability of human-level AI within 10, 20, or 50 years," and compare that to giving them fixed probabilities, like "in what year would you say there's a 10%, 50%, or 90% chance," the answers don't line up the way they should if people had one coherent distribution in their heads. The fixed-years framing tends to produce noticeably later timelines. Put loosely, if you ask "what's the chance by 2040?" people give a smaller number than you'd expect from asking "when is it 50% likely?"

So we ask both ways and randomize which respondents get which. That shows us the framing effect, and it means we don't just report whichever number our format happened to produce. When we aggregate, we combine them, which hopefully averages out some of the bias.

I think it's also an important finding in its own right. These are some of the most knowledgeable people about AI in the world, and their stated forecasts move a lot depending on how you phrase the question. That suggests people haven't thought about it very carefully, or that the question is just really hard. Either way, we should hold any single headline number loosely. The disagreement between framings is part of what we're measuring.

r001.rationale: It says the fixed-years format tends to produce noticeably later timelines than the fixed-probabilities format.

r002.rationale: It says the formats are combined to average out bias, but does not state that the probability distributions derived from the two formats are averaged.

fable-5.1.text:
So the short answer is that we found, somewhat to our surprise, that people give pretty different answers depending on which way you ask the question, and that difference is itself informative.

The two framings are what we call "fixed years" and "fixed probabilities." In the fixed-years version you say, "What's the probability that we have high-level machine intelligence by 2040? By 2060? By 2100?" In the fixed-probabilities version you flip it: "In what year do you think there's a ten percent chance? A fifty percent chance? A ninety percent chance?" In principle these are asking for the same cumulative distribution, just sampling it from different directions, so if people had a coherent picture in their heads you'd get roughly the same curve either way.

What we actually see is that when you give people years and ask for probabilities, their forecasts come out noticeably later than when you give them probabilities and ask for years. The fixed-probabilities framing produces more optimistic, or at least sooner, timelines, and the gap isn't small. We've seen it consistently across multiple rounds of the survey.

So there are a couple of reasons for doing both. One is just honesty about the measurement. If we only used one framing, we'd be reporting a number that looks precise but is actually shifted by an artifact of how the question was worded, and we wouldn't even know it. By asking both ways we can show people the spread and say, here's the range of what experts believe, and here's how much of that range comes from framing rather than from genuine disagreement.

The other reason is that the inconsistency tells you something about the forecasts themselves. If researchers' intuitions about this were well-formed and stable, the framing shouldn't matter much. The fact that it does is a signal that people don't have very precise models here, that they're reaching for something uncertain, and that we should treat any single headline number with a fair amount of humility. I think that's actually one of the more useful things the survey communicates: not just what the median forecast is, but how soft it is.

And then practically, having both lets us combine them. When we report an aggregate, we can pool the answers from the two framings rather than privileging one, which hopefully lands somewhere closer to what people actually believe than either framing alone would.

r001.rationale: It says forecasts from the years-then-probabilities format come out noticeably later than forecasts from the probabilities-then-years format.

r002.rationale: It says the answers can be pooled, but does not state that the probability distributions derived from the two formats are averaged.

astra-6.text:
We ask both ways because the way you frame the question seems to affect the answer quite a lot. You can ask, “What’s the probability of human-level AI by 2050?” Or you can ask, “In what year is there a 50 percent chance of human-level AI?” In principle, those are two ways of eliciting the same underlying distribution. But in practice, they give us different timelines.

One possibility is that people anchor on the numbers you give them. If you supply years, those years influence which timelines they consider; if you supply probabilities, that encourages a different way of thinking about it. We don’t know that one framing is reliably better, so using both lets us see how sensitive the results are to the question format, rather than treating the answer to one particular wording as a precise measure of what people believe.

r001.rationale: The response says the two formats produce different timelines, but does not state that supplying years and asking for probabilities produces later forecasts.

r002.rationale: It says using both formats reveals sensitivity to wording, but does not describe averaging the probability distributions derived from them.

sol-6.1.text:
We ask both ways because the framing seems to affect the answers quite a lot. You can ask, “What’s the probability of human-level AI by 2050?” Or you can ask, “In what year do you think there’s a 50% chance of human-level AI?” In principle, those should give you consistent points on the same probability distribution. In practice, they don’t necessarily do that.

People tend to give later timelines when you give them probabilities and ask for years than when you give them years and ask for probabilities. We don’t really know which framing produces better forecasts, so using both lets us see how sensitive the results are to the way we ask the question, rather than presenting one framing as though it gives a uniquely reliable answer.

r001.rationale: The response says the probabilities-then-years format produces later timelines, the opposite of the criterion.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe averaging probability distributions from the two formats.
